title: Gobble Gobble: Turkeys!
summary: Josh and Chuck explore wild turkeys for Thanksgiving: Ben Franklin's preference for the turkey as national emblem, the two species and their range from North America to Central and South America (ocellated turkeys), physical traits (snood, carunclesc, dewlap, beards, spurs), habitat and diet, daily routine of feeding and roosting, keen sight and hearing, mating displays and lek behavior, nesting, poult development and alarm calls, social flocks, the turkey-and-dog video, turkey vocalizations, the myth of turkeys drowning in rain, memory and intelligence, how to haze turkeys off a property, and a Thanksgiving turkey-consumption statistic. Also covers the documentary Vernon, Florida and its subject Henry Ships. The episode closes with listener mail from Erica about pronunciation of scientific terms and the 'the' before California highway numbers.

segments.title: Opening banter and Vernon, Florida reference
segments.summary: Josh opens with an apology for quoting Henry Ships from the documentary Vernon, Florida, credits the Humane Society article as the main research source, and jokes about giving up turkey.

segments.title: Ben Franklin and the turkey as national emblem
segments.summary: Franklin preferred the turkey to the bald eagle as national bird, calling the eagle lazy and a thief; the hosts note male turkeys' red, white and blue head coloring and that there are two species, with the common turkey in North America and ocellated turkeys in Central America.

segments.title: Turkey appearance, sexes, and life stage names
segments.summary: Describes ocellated turkey appearance, names for gobblers, Jakes, hens and poults, adult weights, and facial features: caruncles, snood, and dewlap, plus the beard and spurs on males.

segments.title: Turkey habitat, range, and diet
segments.summary: Turkeys prefer mature forests with mast-bearing trees near grassy edges, roost in trees at night, have home ranges that vary with food availability, and eat a wide range of foods including insects, which poults rely on early. They get water from vegetation and snow.

segments.title: Daily routine, digestion, and senses
segments.summary: Turkeys are diurnal, feed, dust bathe, and rest, then run or fly back to roost before dark. They swallow food whole and use gizzard stones to grind it. Their sight is strong (wide field of vision, color vision), with excellent hearing that compensates for poor depth perception.

segments.title: Henry Ships, hunting difficulty, and turkey mating
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how hard turkeys are to hunt because of their hearing and wariness, Henry Ships's love of hunting, the spring gobbling peaks, polygamy, harem and lek mating systems, and the role of Jakes and dominance in mating.

segments.title: Nesting, incubation, poult hatching, and parthenogenesis
segments.summary: Hens lay eggs one per day in grassy areas at forest edges, incubate them, and communicate with the chicks before hatching. Poults use an egg tooth, learn their mother's alarm call, freeze when alarmed, and can fly after about 17 days. Parthenogenesis is noted as rare and produces only males.

segments.title: Turkey flocks, social bonds, and turkey and dog video
segments.summary: Turkeys form social flocks, merge into large mega flocks, adopt orphaned poults, and show distress when separated from their flock. A video of a turkey living with a dog is mentioned.

segments.title: Vocalizations, purring, myths, memory, and hazing
segments.summary: Covers turkey calls including tree yelp, plain yelp, cluck, alarm putt, kee kee, and cackle; purring; the myth that turkeys drown in rain (linked to seizures in factory-farmed birds); their memory and face recognition; and hazing methods to deter them from property. Closes with the Thanksgiving consumption statistic and listener mail from Erica about pronunciation and the 'the' before California highway numbers.
